articles.title: Iran honour killing: Parents beat, strangle pregnant teenage daughter to death
articles.summary: A 19-year-old pregnant woman has been killed by her parents in an alleged honour killing in Iran, with rights groups saying she was beaten and strangled
articles.body: A 19-year-old pregnant woman has been killed by her parents in an alleged honour killing in Iran, with rights groups saying she was beaten and strangled after telling her family she was two months pregnant.Police in the western Iranian city of Sanandaj have arrested the parents of Helia Fattahi on charges of killing their daughter, the Iran International reported.Both allegedly confessed during questioning, Shahram Abdi, head of the criminal police in Kordestan province, said on Tuesday.Detectives visited the family’s home after receiving a report of a young woman's death and concluded that she had been murdered, Abdi said.Police cited “family disputes” as the motive but did not comment on Fattahi’s pregnancy or how she was killed. Fattahi was killed on Saturday night at her family’s home in the Naysar neighbourhood of Sanandaj, Iran International reported, citing rights group Hengaw.According to the group, she had disclosed her pregnancy to her family the previous week, following a relationship with a young man. Her parents allegedly beat her before strangling her.Hengaw and another rights group, Hana, described the killing as a so-called honour killing. However, reports differed on her age, with police and Hengaw identifying her as 19, while Hana said she was 16.Third killing of a young woman in a weekFattahi's death is the third killing of a young woman or girl in Iran in a little over a week to draw widespread attention.Earlier, on November 18, 23-year-old Sadaf Haghbin was shot dead at her birthday party in Gilan province in northern Iran. Iranian media reported that her former boyfriend was the gunman and allegedly killed her after she refused to marry him.Days earlier, 16-year-old schoolgirl Sogand Sayadi died after falling from the fifth floor of a building in Kermanshah.A national network of teachers’ unions said Sayadi had warned school staff that her father would kill her if they sent her home with him. The coroner said she died from injuries sustained in the fall, while the provincial prosecutor said the circumstances were being investigated.At least 84 women and girls were killed in Iran between March 21 and October 13, with 75 of the cases involving perpetrators known to the victims, according to a tally of media-reported killings cited by Iran International.Twelve of the victims were under 18, and eight were killed by their fathers, brothers or other blood relatives. The figures cover only cases reported by the media.Ahead of Wednesday's International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, Hana said it was alarmed by the rise in recorded killings of women in Iran.The rights group said the absence of transparent data and the large number of unreported domestic violence cases made it impossible to determine the true scale of the problem. It called for women at risk to have access to safe shelters and legal protection.A bill aimed at protecting women from violence has been shuttled between the government, parliament and other state bodies for more than 15 years but has yet to become law.Under Article 301 of Iran's Islamic Penal Code, fathers and paternal grandfathers who kill their children are exempt from qisas, or retribution in kind, which is the punishment prescribed for most murders. The exemption does not extend to mothers.Following Sayadi’s death, lawyers and women’s rights activists called for changes to the law and stronger legal protections for women.The latest killing comes amid growing scrutiny of Iran’s treatment of women, including its punishment of female performers who defy restrictions.Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi, 29, and four members of her concert team were flogged 74 times each in Qom on Monday for performing without a head covering, a defence lawyer told the BBC.Ahmadi was punished for performing in a sleeveless dress with her hair uncovered during an online concert in December 2024, defying Iran’s mandatory hijab rules.Iranian authorities subsequently opened a case against Ahmadi and members of her production team over an “illegal concert”. Women have been banned from singing solo in public in Iran since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Telangana Rising Global Summit 2026 to spotlight five agriculture clusters—food processing, AI, seeds, FMCG and agri-entrepreneurship—to attract investments.
articles.body: Hyderabad: Five agriculture-focused clusters covering food processing, artificial intelligence, seeds, FMCG and farmer entrepreneurship will be in focus at the Telangana Rising Global Summit 2026, with the state govt seeking to attract investments across the farm-to-market value chain.Five dedicated sessions will explore ways to add value to agricultural produce through food processing, use of AI in food systems, strengthening Telangana’s position as India’s seed hub, developing FMCG and food brands, and transforming farmers into agri-entrepreneurs.Agriculture minister Tummala Nageswara Rao announced this at a meeting of the executive council for agriculture, fertilizers, FMCG and food processing sectors at the secretariat on Wednesday. The summit will be held at Bharat Future City from Dec 7 to 9.A special agriculture expo spread across 1,904 square metres will also be organised under the theme ‘Farm to Fork’. It will showcase seeds, agricultural inputs, modern technology, mechanisation equipment, infrastructure, processed food products, FMCG brands and startups.Tummala said the govt wanted to connect agriculture, fertilizer production, food processing and FMCG manufacturing to build an integrated value chain. The focus would be on processing farm produce within Telangana, converting it into branded products and taking them to domestic and international markets.He said this would help farmers secure better prices while creating employment opportunities in rural areas. articles.title: Iowa residents told to take shelter as US Army prepares to detonate 5 tonnes of explosives; toxic dust feared
articles.summary: Residents of a small town in Iowa are being asked to take shelter indoors and keep their windows shut as the US Army prepares to detonate nearly five
articles.body: Residents of a small town in Iowa are being asked to take shelter indoors and keep their windows shut as the US Army prepares to detonate nearly five tonnes of unstable explosives at a nearby military ammunition plant on Wednesday, raising fears of toxic lead dust spreading across parts of the state and neighbouring Missouri.The controlled blast, scheduled for around 10 am ET, will destroy 9,700lb (4,400kg) of lead azide, a highly volatile compound used in military ammunition and explosives, stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a southeastern Iowa town with around 400 residents.The explosion could release plumes of toxic lead dust across a 100-mile (160km) radius. The projected path of the airborne material has shifted with changing weather conditions. The Army's latest forecast indicates that the plume could move southwest of Middletown and extend into northern Missouri.In a public safety advisory, the Army urged people in affected areas, particularly children, pregnant women and those with chronic illnesses, to avoid outdoor activities until further guidance is issued."A more precise time will be communicated after evaluating changing weather patterns and waiting for the safest possible conditions," the Army said on Tuesday.According to CNN, Army officials maintain that a controlled detonation is the safest available option because the lead azide has deteriorated and become dangerously unstable. Officials warned that colder temperatures or attempts to open the containers for chemical neutralisation could trigger an uncontrolled explosion.Residents warned as toxic dust could spread across statesAuthorities have advised people living within 20 miles of the ammunition plant to remain indoors with windows closed to reduce exposure to airborne lead dust, noise and vibration. Some residents within five miles southwest of the facility could also be asked to evacuate.The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is supporting temporary relocation for residents of Middletown and surrounding areas considered at risk.FEMA administrator Cameron Hamilton said residents in the southwest direction had been offered relocation assistance, including transportation, accommodation, meals and other essential services.Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds has also declared a disaster emergency in Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren counties. The Iowa National Guard is preparing to deploy up to 100 soldiers to assist with public safety and community outreach.The operation was initially scheduled for last Friday but was postponed three times amid growing public opposition and legal challenges from environmental groups.Court allows Army to proceed despite environmental concernsThe planned detonation faced a legal challenge over concerns that the explosion could disperse toxic lead dust and create long-term environmental and health risks.A three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit ruled on Monday that the Army could proceed with the operation, allowing an emergency permit issued by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to remain in place. The court found that the EPA had incorporated safeguards aimed at minimising the spread of dust.CNN reported that an attorney representing one of the environmental groups involved in the lawsuit said the legal battle was not entirely over.Michael Schmidt, an attorney with the Iowa Environmental Council, told CNN's Kaitlan Collins that the lawsuit had questioned the adequacy of the EPA's emergency permit, including provisions for the aftermath of the explosion and the clean-up process.At a press conference on Tuesday, acting US Army Secretary Adam Telle said officials had been unable to identify a viable alternative to destroying the unstable material."There is consensus across experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said.Senator-elect Josh Turek criticised the circumstances that led to the chemicals deteriorating to such a dangerous condition, saying there had been a failure of transparency and communication.The Army has maintained that the controlled blast is necessary to eliminate the risk posed by the unstable stockpile.You use AI every day.
